stances.claim: The six Scotus conservatives ('textualists' or 'originalists') 'flexed their super muscles' and issued three landmark June 2022 decisions, by uniform 6-3 votes, that 'asserted their absolute supremacy in construing the US Constitution' -- Dobbs (Alito, abortion), Kennedy v. Bremerton (Gorsuch, religious expression), and NY v. Bruen (Thomas, bear arms).

Scotus has historically divided philosophically into conservatives (originalism + textualism, battle cry 'Verba legis') and liberals/progressives (living-Constitution doctrine prioritizing intent and growth over words and punctuation) -- and Republican vs Democratic presidents reliably appoint accordingly.

President Trump's three appointments (Gorsuch 2017, Kavanaugh 2018, Barrett 2020 -- the last filling Ginsburg's seat after her Sept 18, 2020 death) transformed a fragile 5-4 conservative edge (often broken by Kennedy or Roberts swing votes) into a 'commanding 6-3 majority.' 'Though much vilified, he was able to name three Scotus justices. In this sense, his legacy is a conservative Scotus that changed, and will continue to change, the constitutional landscape in the US.'

Dobbs v. Jackson completely reversed Roe v. Wade (Jan 22, 1973), holding that 'The Constitution does not confer a right to abortion' while leaving federal and state legislatures free to enact such a right. Roe was condemned as 'egregiously wrong... Without any grounding in the constitutional text, history or precedent.'

From the originalist perspective, the right to abortion under Roe was an artifact of 'judicial fiat' -- extracted from the due-process clause's protection of 'life, liberty, or property' -- precisely the kind of extra-textual interpretation textualism rejects.

Philippine doctrine is unambiguous on the abortion question: Imbong v. Ochoa (April 8, 2014, 14-1) ruled that 'life begins at fertilization, not at implantation' -- and CJ adds 'in my humble opinion, abortion can be committed as early as fertilization because life begins at fertilization.'

notable_anecdotes: The conservative-roster genealogy preserved with appointing-presidents: CJ Roberts (Bush Jr. 2005), Thomas (Bush Sr. 1991), Alito (Bush Jr. 2006), Gorsuch (Trump 2017), Kavanaugh (Trump 2018), Barrett (Trump 2020) -- and the liberal triad: Breyer (Clinton 1994), Sotomayor (Obama 2009), Kagan (Obama 2010). Modeling civic-pedagogical thoroughness on Scotus composition.

Amy Coney Barrett identified as a 'self-confessed follower and former law clerk of the late Justice Antonin Scalia, who, for several decades, was the recognized leader of the conservatives' -- preserving the doctrinal-inheritance lineage from Scalia through Barrett.

Scotus's own self-condemning quotation of Roe -- 'Roe was egregiously wrong... Without any grounding in the constitutional text, history or precedent, Roe imposed on the entire country a detailed set of rules for pregnancy divided into trimesters' -- preserved verbatim as the new majority's own institutional voice.

CJ's closing position-disclosure on abortion at fertilization -- 'in my humble opinion, abortion can be committed as early as fertilization because life begins at fertilization' -- anchored to Imbong v. Ochoa (April 8, 2014, 14-1) as the Philippine doctrinal counter-point to Roe.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the three landmark June 2022 Scotus 6-3 decisions through which the six conservatives ('textualists' or 'originalists') 'flexed their super muscles and asserted their absolute supremacy in construing the US Constitution': Dobbs v. Jackson (June 24, Alito) abolishing the right to abortion; Kennedy v. Bremerton (June 27, Gorsuch) protecting a government employee's personal religious observance from government reprisal; and New York v. Bruen (June 23, Thomas) strengthening the right to keep and bear arms in public for self-defense. He sketches the philosophical map: conservatives believe in originalism (interpret Constitution by framers' original intent) and textualism (interpret laws by the words used, battle cry 'Verba legis'), while liberals/progressives believe in a 'living Constitution' that 'grows with time, solves the vagaries of the present, and anticipates the needs of the future,' relying on intent over words. For about 100 years the Scotus was roughly even; the last two decades saw a fragile 5-4 conservative edge often flipped by Justice Anthony Kennedy or CJ John Roberts. Trump's three appointments (Gorsuch 2017, Kavanaugh 2018, and Amy Coney Barrett 2020 after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's September 18, 2020 death -- Barrett was a self-confessed follower and former law clerk of the late conservative leader Antonin Scalia) produced a 'commanding 6-3 majority.' CJ preserves the full lineage: conservatives CJ Roberts (Bush Jr. 2005), Thomas (Bush Sr. 1991), Alito (Bush Jr. 2006), Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett; liberals Breyer (Clinton 1994), Sotomayor and Kagan (Obama 2009 and 2010). He notes: 'Though much vilified, he was able to name three Scotus justices. In this sense, his legacy is a conservative Scotus that changed, and will continue to change, the constitutional landscape in the US.' He devotes the remaining space to Dobbs, which completely reversed Roe v. Wade (January 22, 1973, 7-2, Harry Blackmun) -- Roe had extracted a right to privacy 'by judicial fiat' from the due-process clause ('nor shall any state deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law'), and was narrowed but not overturned by Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), Whole Woman's Health (2016), and June Medical Services (2020). Dobbs now holds that 'The Constitution does not confer a right to abortion,' though federal or state legislatures may enact such laws; the Scotus 'roared' that 'Roe was egregiously wrong... Without any grounding in the constitutional text, history or precedent, Roe imposed on the entire country a detailed set of rules for pregnancy divided into trimesters.' Philippine doctrine is unambiguous in the opposite direction: Imbong v. Ochoa (April 8, 2014, 14-1) ruled that 'life begins at fertilization, not at implantation' -- and CJ concludes, 'in my humble opinion, abortion can be committed as early as fertilization because life begins at fertilization.'
